item.title: (no title)
item.content:encoded:
Full disclosure: I remember what this used to be, and part of me wants to give it the Nobel Peace Prize for not being Bush 2, if you know what I mean. In spite of that, I think that this is good enough to stand on it's own.

I particularly like that she's not static, that her psychological condition is progressing (though not in a good direction) because it reinforces the idea that she's not a doll, she's a young girl with severe trauma in both her past and present, and that the Foundation isn't her glass case. It removes the "neatness" from the whole Living Doll concept, and I like what that does for the story.

It's also well-written overall, though I think replacing "undesirable" with "undesired" or something similar would let it read a bit better. "Undesirable" sounds to me like more of an objective valuation in context, but it's specifically the subject's perspective that's being referenced. This is certainly a nitpick, though.

As far as the videotape transcript seeming cliche' goes, I'm not about to tell anyone that how it strikes them isn't how it strikes them, but it rang true for me, for what that's worth.

I'm glad to see this saved from what it was. +1

item.content:encoded:
*pokes Wikidot with a sharp stick*

Edit:

[…] the implication that her delusion about the event […] has taken on physical reality on account of her being around a bunch of broken porcelain at the time of trauma […]

This… isn't quite right, and if it didn't come across well, then that may certainly be my fault. Abigail's mother had her in child pageants since she was a toddler, doting on her due to her inability to have any more children. The desire to be a doll was already there; daddy hates her, but not her mommy's dolls. Mommy dresses her like a doll, so why not be a doll?

The porcelain wasn't happenstance. She was eating them, maybe because she just chose for all this to happen and maybe because she just wanted to die. Who knows what really happened? She's certainly not going to tell us, her mind is broken.

item.title: (no title)
item.content:encoded:
I don't like it.

You successfully got rid of the creep factor and brought the tone up to standards, but I don't like the story. The video recording of the domestic dispute is way too cliche, and the young girl's reaction to it is also (even Star Trek TNG has an episode where a guilt-ridden little boy develops a delusion of being an Android to cope with his belief that he killed his family and a whole space station. It's been done).

What's more, the implication that her delusion about the event (I am a doll. I am perfect and pretty so Mommy will love me and Daddy will love her and everything is fine) has taken on physical reality on account of her being around a bunch of broken porcelain at the time of trauma is… weak. Trauma being connected to the supernatural is like the grandaddy of all horror cliches.

Your clinical tone is good, and your containment procedures are appropriate, but the way you've re-imagined the concept and the story doesn't do anything good for me.

-1
